problem.title: Retail demand forecasting
problem.context: A retailer forecasts weekly demand per store and product: 400 stores and 30,000 products. Every Monday the forecasts for the next eight weeks feed the replenishment system, which orders stock. Sales from the tills reach the company's data warehouse every night; promotions and public holidays move demand strongly. A team of three data scientists owns the forecasting pipeline end to end. The data warehouse is run by the central IT department, which the team cannot change.

requirements.text: Produce, every week, the forecast per store and product for the next eight weeks, and deliver it to the replenishment system by Monday 06:00.
Run the forecast again for any past week exactly as it was produced.
Try new model ideas and compare them with the production model on past weeks before they replace it.
Asked for the forecast of a week up to two years back, the team produces the same numbers within one working day.
A new model idea that beats the production model on past weeks reaches production within one week, with no manual step except the approval.
When a weekly run fails, the team is told within 15 minutes, and the replenishment system never receives a partial forecast.
A new team member can run the whole pipeline on their own machine within their first week.
Three data scientists, with no data engineers; the data warehouse stays as it is.
The weekly run must fit in the six hours between the nightly load and the Monday deadline.

values: Compute: Managed distributed batch

Delivery: Stage complete output and atomically publish
Experiment: Versioned backtests with manual packaging and deployment
points.description: A managed distributed batch process trains one global model across retail series using promotion and holiday features. Immutable snapshots make inputs, features, code, and models reproducible; outputs are staged and atomically published, while versioned backtests inform manually packaged and deployed experiments. Trade-off: This gains reproducibility, scalable training, and consistent releases, but gives up rapid iteration and low-latency updates because runs and deployments are batch-oriented and manual. Manual packaging also adds operational effort and opportunities for deployment error.

points.description: A managed VM runs batch forecasts using separate models for defined product and store groups. It reads immutable raw extracts with pinned code, stages the complete forecast output, and atomically publishes it; versioned backtests support manually packaged and deployed experiments. Trade-off: This favors reproducibility, controlled releases, and consistent published results. It gives up elastic scaling and deployment speed, while segmentation, manual packaging, and a single VM increase operational effort and may constrain throughput.

values: Compute: Warehouse SQL plus single VM
Model: Independent per-series models
History: Requery current warehouse data
Delivery: Write forecasts directly to replenishment tables

points.description: A single VM would query current warehouse data with SQL, fit an independent forecasting model for each series, and generate forecasts. Manual scripts and backtests would support experimentation, while the resulting forecasts would be written directly into replenishment tables. Trade-off: This is straightforward and uses current data with a direct operational path, but single-VM compute and per-series models may limit scale and increase maintenance. Requerying and direct table writes weaken reproducibility and couple forecasting closely to replenishment data.

points.description: Managed distributed batch jobs train a global model and category/store residual adjustments from versioned input snapshots. Trade-off: This improves reproducibility, scalable processing, and protection against partial or unvalidated releases. It gives up fresher, lower-latency updates and adds storage, batch orchestration, residual-maintenance, and approval overhead.

adrs.title: Where should weekly forecasting compute run?
adrs.context: The pipeline must score 12 million store-product series after the nightly load and finish inside six hours. Three data scientists must operate it, and the centrally run warehouse cannot be changed. A single VM is approachable but has limited throughput headroom; distributed managed compute offers capacity with more platform surface to learn.

options.name: Managed distributed batch
values: Compute: Managed distributed batch
pros: Can spread large training and scoring jobs across workers.
Keeps warehouse ownership and configuration unchanged.
cons: Adds orchestration and onboarding work for a small team.
Six-hour runtime and local setup still require validation.
options.reason: All retained alternatives use this execution path because it has the most capacity headroom for the deadline while leaving warehouse operations alone.

options.name: Single managed VM
values: Compute: Single managed VM batch
pros: A compact environment is easier to understand and run.
Fewer execution components may help first-week onboarding.
cons: A single host is a throughput bottleneck for 12 million series.
Provides little headroom for the six-hour window.
options.reason: The approach changed to distributed batch after the single-host throughput risk became clear.

options.name: Warehouse SQL with one VM
values: Compute: Warehouse SQL plus single VM
pros: Uses familiar warehouse queries and simple scripts.
cons: Leaves per-series computation on one host and mutable warehouse data undermines replay.
options.reason: This approach missed the scale and replay requirements.

adrs.title: How should forecasts share information across series?
adrs.context: Promotions and holidays strongly affect demand across stores and products, while series differ locally. The model must cover a very large series count, permit historical comparisons, and remain practical for a small team to maintain. A single pooled model is simpler to operate; segmentation and local corrections can represent differences but add model management.

options.name: Pooled global model with known demand drivers
values: Model: Global pooled model with promotion and holiday features
pros: Shares information across many series.
Uses promotion and holiday signals directly.
Keeps one principal model path for backtesting and maintenance.
cons: May miss local category or store residual patterns.
options.reason: This is the simpler scalable modeling choice where promotion and holiday effects are explicit.

options.name: Segmented product and store group models
values: Model: Segmented models by product and store groups
pros: Allows distinct group behavior and comparisons.
cons: Increases model inventory and operational maintenance.
options.reason: This alternative favors local model fit and preserves direct model-to-model backtesting.

options.name: Global model with category and store residual adjustments
values: Model: Global model with category and store residual adjustments
pros: Shares broad patterns while adding local correction capacity.
cons: Residual stages add complexity and may increase run time.
options.reason: This balances global learning with category/store-specific adjustment, subject to scale and maintenance validation.

options.name: Independent model for each series
values: Model: Independent per-series models
pros: Allows every series its own model behavior.
cons: Creates a large model inventory and high compute burden.
options.reason: The single-host form did not fit the scale or six-hour deadline.

adrs.title: How should historical inputs and run artifacts be retained?
adrs.context: The team must rerun any forecast from up to two years ago and reproduce the same numbers within one working day. Current warehouse data can change after the original run. Retaining frozen input snapshots and code/model artifacts costs storage and requires lifecycle management, while requerying current data cannot guarantee the original run's inputs.

options.name: Freeze all run artifacts
values: History: Immutable input, feature, code, and model snapshots
pros: Captures data, transformations, code, and model needed for exact replay.
cons: Requires storage retention and artifact management.
options.reason: This most directly supports exact replay of the same output.

options.name: Retain raw extracts and pinned code
values: History: Immutable raw extracts and pinned code snapshots
pros: Preserves source values and transformation version for reruns.
cons: Feature and model artifact handling needs explicit implementation.
options.reason: This lightweight artifact set covers repeatable input and code for the segmented approach.

options.name: Keep versioned input snapshots in object storage
values: History: Versioned input snapshots in object storage
pros: Provides a durable historical data source outside the warehouse.
cons: Code, feature, and model versions must also be associated with each run.
options.reason: This gives the hybrid approach a durable replay input while keeping warehouse changes out of scope.

options.name: Requery current warehouse data
values: History: Requery current warehouse data
pros: Avoids a separate input snapshot store.
cons: Later warehouse changes can change historical outputs.
options.reason: This fails the exact replay requirement.

adrs.title: How should a run reach replenishment and how should models be promoted?
adrs.context: The handoff must finish by Monday 06:00 and must never expose a partial forecast. New models must be compared on past weeks and move to production within a week after approval. Staging and an atomic promotion protect downstream consumers; automated backtests reduce manual work, but a robust release pipeline requires setup.
